items.title: 4.2 Work done by a variable force

source_refs.note: Topic 4.2 with Figs. 4.5 to 4.8 and Example 4.1 (PDF 76-78, printed 73-75).

blocks.text: In many cases the force does not remain constant during the process of doing work. For example, as a rocket moves away from the Earth, work is done against the force of gravity, which varies as the inverse square of the distance from the Earth's centre. Similarly, the force exerted by a spring increases with the amount of stretch. How can we calculate the work done in such situations?

Figure 4.5 shows the path of a particle in the x y plane as it moves from point P to point Q. The path has been divided into n short intervals of displacements Δd₁, Δd₂, ……, Δdₙ and F₁, F₂, ……, Fₙ are the forces acting during these intervals.

blocks.alt: A curved path from point P up to point Q is cut by tick marks into short intervals delta d1, delta d2 ... delta dn. Force F1 acts at P at an angle theta1 to the path, and force F2 acts at the start of the second interval at an angle theta2.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.5: A particle acted upon by a variable force, moves along the path shown from point P to point Q (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.5).

blocks.text: During each small interval, the force is supposed to be approximately constant. So, the work done for the first interval can then be written as

blocks.text_alt: ΔW₁ = F₁ · Δd₁ = F₁ cos θ₁ Δd₁
ΔW₂ = F₂ · Δd₂ = F₂ cos θ₂ Δd₂

blocks.text: and so on. The total work done in moving the object can be calculated by adding all these terms.

blocks.latex: = F_1\cos\theta_1\,\Delta d_1 + F_2\cos\theta_2\,\Delta d_2 + \dots + F_n\cos\theta_n\,\Delta d_n
blocks.text_alt: = F₁ cos θ₁ Δd₁ + F₂ cos θ₂ Δd₂ + …… + Fₙ cos θₙ Δdₙ
or   W_total = Σ (i = 1 to n) Fᵢ cos θᵢ Δdᵢ   (4.4)

blocks.text: We can examine this graphically by plotting F cos θ verses d as shown in Fig. 4.6. The displacement d has been sub-divided into the same n equal intervals. The value of F cos θ at the beginning of each interval is indicated in the figure.

blocks.alt: A graph of F cos theta against d with origin O and axes x and y. From P to Q the displacement is divided into equal intervals delta d1, delta d2 ... delta di ... delta dn. Each shaded strip has the height of F cos theta at the beginning of its interval, marked F1 cos theta1, Fi cos theta i and Fn cos theta n; the smooth curve runs over them.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.6: F cos theta against d, divided into n equal intervals (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.6).

blocks.text: Now the iᵗʰ shaded rectangle has an area Fᵢ cos θᵢ Δdᵢ which is the work done during the iᵗʰ interval. Thus, the work done given by Eq. 4.4 equals the sum of the areas of all the rectangles. If we sub-divide the distance into a large number of intervals so that each Δd becomes very small, the work done given by Eq. 4.4 becomes more accurate. If we let each Δd to approach zero, then we obtain an exact result for the work done, such as:

blocks.text_alt: W_total = Limit (Δd → 0) Σ (i = 1 to n) Fᵢ cos θᵢ Δdᵢ   (4.5)

blocks.text: If this limit Δd approaches zero, the total area of the rectangles (Fig. 4.6) approaches the area between the F cos θ verses d curve and x-axis from P to Q as shown shaded in Fig. 4.7.

blocks.alt: A graph of F cos theta against Displacement d with origin O. The whole region under the smooth curve between P and Q is shaded, with dashed vertical lines at P and Q.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.7: The area under the F cos theta against d curve between P and Q (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.7).

blocks.text: Thus, the work done by a variable force in moving a particle between two points is equal to the area under the F cos θ verses d curve between the two points P and Q as shown in Fig. 4.7.

blocks.title: Example 4.1
blocks.problem: A force F acting on an object varies with distance d as shown in Fig. 4.8. Calculate the work done by the force as the object moves from d = 0 to d = 6 m.
steps: The work done by the force is equal to the total area under the curve from d = 0 to d = 6 m. This area is equal to the area of the rectangular section from d = 0 to d = 4 m, plus the area of triangular section from d = 4 m to d = 6 m.
Work done represented by the area of rectangle = 4 m × 5 N = 20 N m = 20 J
Work done represented by the area of triangle = ½ × 2 m × 5 N = 5 N m = 5 J
blocks.answer: Therefore, the total work done = 20 J + 5 J = 25 J

blocks.alt: A graph of F in newtons (0 to 5) against d in metres (0 to 6). The force is 5 N from d = 0 to d = 4 m, then falls in a straight line to zero at d = 6 m. The rectangle from 0 to 4 m and the triangle from 4 to 6 m under the graph are shaded in two colours.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.8: Force against distance for Example 4.1 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.8).
